issues.legal_issue: A High Court exercising broad revisionary powers may differ from concurrent findings of the lower courts.
material_facts: The tenant challenged the High Court’s decision to differ from the concurrent conclusions of the trial court and the District Judge.
The revision provision authorized the High Court to examine the record concerning the legality or correctness of the decision or proceeding and to pass an appropriate order.
issues.conclusion: The challenge to the High Court’s authority to differ from the concurrent findings was rejected because the revisionary powers were couched in wide terms.
issues.legal_principle: Section 50 of the Mysore Rent Control Act, 1961 empowered the High Court to call for and examine the record to satisfy itself as to the legality or correctness of a decision, order, or proceeding and to pass such order as it thought fit. The Court relied on the breadth of that provision; it cited no earlier case on this issue.

predicates.rent_control_revision_proceeding: The matter came before the High Court in revision from a decision in a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.high_court_has_broad_record_review_power: The governing revision process authorized the High Court to examine the record for the legality or correctness of the decision or proceeding and to make an appropriate order.
predicates.lower_courts_reached_concurrent_findings: The trial court and the intermediate appellate court reached the same conclusion on the disputed matter.

issues.definition: When a rent-control matter reaches the High Court in revision under a process granting broad record-review powers, the High Court may reassess findings shared by the lower courts.

issues.legal_issue: In deciding comparative hardship in an eviction claim based on the landlord’s reasonable and bona fide need, the court must weigh the relevant evidence and circumstances of both landlord and tenant rather than place the entire burden on the tenant.
material_facts: The landlord sought the tenant’s business premises for use as a godown for a nearby hotel and already had other space used for storage.
The tenant had conducted business at the premises for many years and gave evidence that losing the premises would seriously disrupt that business.

The trial court and District Judge considered the tenant likely to suffer greater hardship, while the High Court treated the tenant as bearing the burden of proving greater hardship and found that burden unmet.

The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had focused on the burden of proof instead of considering the entire evidence and remanded the matter for reconsideration, permitting further evidence if appropriate.
issues.conclusion: The appeal was allowed and the matter remanded to the High Court to decide comparative hardship by considering all the circumstances and relevant evidence, including the availability of other reasonable accommodation for both sides.
issues.legal_principle: Section 21(1)(h) of the Mysore Rent Control Act, 1961 required the landlord to prove reasonable and bona fide need. Section 21(4) barred eviction where, considering all circumstances—including other reasonable accommodation available to landlord or tenant—greater hardship would result from granting the decree than refusing it. Both parties must adduce relevant evidence, and the court must assess that evidence together; proof of the landlord’s need does not shift the entire burden to the tenant. The Court rejected the broad burden proposition in Madhadevappa v. Mallavva. It discussed Kelley v. Goodwin and Smith v. Penny, which arose under a different English statute, but emphasized that the courts there had considered the entire evidence.

predicates.rent_eviction_based_on_landlord_need: The proceeding concerns eviction sought on the ground that the landlord reasonably and bona fide needs the premises for occupation.
predicates.landlord_has_other_accommodation: The landlord already has other accommodation that may be relevant to the claimed need.
predicates.tenant_faces_business_disruption: The tenant uses the premises for business and has evidence that eviction would disrupt that business.
predicates.court_must_determine_comparative_hardshi: The court compares the hardship of granting eviction with the hardship of refusing it after considering relevant evidence and circumstances concerning both landlord and tenant.

issues.definition: When eviction is sought for the landlord’s need and the parties’ available accommodation and potential hardship are in issue, the court must decide comparative hardship by weighing relevant evidence from both sides.
